headlines.title: Couple found dead at Oakland Hills home identified as owners of fashion company
headlines.description: A couple found shot to death outside their Oakland Hills home last week has been identified as Michelle Min and Bryan Walker, police officials announced Monday. The founders of fashion brand Bryn Walker, Min, 63, and Walker, 64, were found outside their home in the 400 block of Panoramic Way, close to the Berkeley border, after a neighbor reported hearing gunshots Friday at about 10:45 a.m. The address is within the Panoramic Hills neighborhood along the border with Berkeley, near the campus of the University of California. Oakland Assistant Police Chief Casey Johnson said at the time that the pair, who appeared to be married, were discovered outdoors after officers responded to a call from a neighbor. A firearm was located at the scene, according to Johnson, who said police had not confirmed if the case was a double murder or murder-suicide. There was no threat to the neighborhood and police weren’t looking for other suspects, Johnson said. The couple owned and operated Bryn Walker, a Berkeley-based fashion design company with retail shops and a wholesale operation that was founded in 1991, according to state businesses license records. Anyone with information about the case can call the Oakland Police Department at 510-238-3821 or the tip line at 510-238-7950. Video and photos can be sent to cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

headlines.title: Morgan Hill man allegedly confesses to killing wife after bringing her to hospital
headlines.description: A Morgan Hill man allegedly showed up at a San Jose hospital Saturday morning and confessed to killing his wife, who was found in a vehicle parked at the hospital and pronounced dead, police said. Morgan Hill police said San Jose police contacted them at about 9:20 a.m. Saturday and said 37-year-old Roy Anthony Lopez arrived at Good Samaritan Hospital in San Jose and said he had killed his wife. First responders later found Lopez’s wife inside a vehicle parked at the hospital, police said. Emergency personnel provided immediate medical care, but the woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Her identity wasn’t immediately known. San Jose police detained Lopez without incident. Morgan Hill police then took him into custody and transported him to Morgan Hill for questioning, police said. He was later booked into jail on suspicion of murder. Citing a preliminary investigation, police said the alleged homicide occurred at a home along the 1100 block of Vintage Lane in Morgan Hill. Police said no firearm was used, but they did not immediately reveal how the woman died. Police said they found the couple’s three children – ages 3, 6 and 14 – in the home and believe they may have witnessed the attack. The children have since been handed over to Santa Clara County’s Department of Family and Children’s Services. Police said the couple was married for more than 10 years. Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact Morgan Hill police Sgt. Sean Bayard by phone at 408-607-3032 or by email at sean.bayard@morganhill.ca.gov. If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline by calling 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), visiting www.thehotline.org or texting LOVEIS to 22522.

headlines.title: Bay Area heat advisory extended through Thursday
headlines.description: Much of the Bay Area is facing hot weather through Thursday, with moderate to major heat risks expected across inland communities, the National Weather Service said Monday. The hottest areas will be inland valleys, where temperatures are expected to reach the mid-80s to low 100s. The forecast calls for highs around 100 degrees in Concord and Livermore, 96 in Napa and Santa Rosa, and 93 in San Jose on Monday. A heat advisory remains in effect through 10 p.m. Thursday for much of the interior Bay Area and Central Coast. The weather service warned that the heat can affect people without adequate cooling or hydration and advised residents to move outdoor activities to cooler parts of the day and never leave people or pets unattended in vehicles. The heat will also raise fire danger in higher terrain through Thursday. Major HeatRisk is expected to remain widespread in parts of the East Bay through Tuesday and across the Santa Clara Valley through Wednesday. Meanwhile, coastal flooding and beach hazards are expected to become a concern beginning Wednesday as high tides push water farther inland along some coastal and bayshore areas. The risks are expected to continue through Sunday. Coastal flooding could affect low-lying roads, parks and trails, while beachgoers should watch for rip currents and sneaker waves. headlines.title: Race for CA insurance commissioner: Once-boring contest is now high stakes
headlines.description: California voters will choose between two Democrats with differing visions for the state’s troubled insurance market when they elect a new insurance commissioner this November. Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor, and Ben Allen, a state senator representing the West Los Angeles region, advanced to the run-off after neither candidate won a majority of the votes in the June primary election. A recent poll showed Kim has nearly 25% of respondents supported Kim while 18% supported Allen. Despite the appearance of Kim’s solid lead, more than 57% of the 1,000 people surveyed said they are undecided. Kim and Allen both seem to agree a major overhaul is needed in California’s insurance system, especially after California has experienced devastating disasters, including wildfires and flooding. But they have a different approach to fixing the current insurance system. One of Kim’s key policy proposals is creating a single-payer disaster insurance system, modeled after programs in New Zealand, Spain and France. While homeowners are free to purchase private policies, the state would provide a guaranteed — automatic and universal — home disaster insurance policy, under Kim’s plan. But critics said Kim’s proposal does not specify how costly and realistic it would be for the state government to operate such a system. Others also worry Kim’s plans would further drive out insurers from California. Allen, whose home was affected in the 2025 Palisades Fire, has a different approach than Kim: the state senator wants to reform the existing insurance system to bring insurers back to California. To make the current model work, Allen wants to “modernize rate-setting,” the process insurers use to calculate premiums based on expected claims, risk factors, operating costs and regulatory requirements. He also wants to make California less vulnerable to future disasters by expanding consumer protections and supporting wildfire-resilient homes and communities. However, Allen’s proposals may make him look like the establishment, not being tough enough on insurers. Critics worry that Allen’s plans would favor insurers over Californians, who have struggled with policy cancelations and high premiums. Elections Sep 30 Kim is endorsed by progressive leaders, such as U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, labor leader David Huerta and outgoing Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis. Allen’s supporters include U.S. senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla as well as California Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas.

headlines.title: New tool aims to make it even easier to be an informed voter
headlines.description: A new tool aims to make it even faster and more convenient for voters to gather election information. OpenBallot.app, started by a group of tech-savvy Bay Area entrepreneurs, allows voters to find information they need to compare candidates and learn about ballot propositions without the paperwork that comes in the mail. “When you go to OpenBallot, right away, boom, you see all the voter guides right there,” OpenBallot.app co-founder Rose Bloomin said. “You don’t have to log in. You don’t have to do anything.” OpenBallot.app is nonpartisan. California voters can access it on their smartphones or computers. Right now, voters can find election information for statewide offices and propositions, as well as local races in San Francisco, Oakland, Berkeley, San Jose, San Diego and Los Angeles. The group hopes to broaden the site to include other cities and other states in the future.

headlines.title: Fatal crash shuts down lanes on northbound I-280 in San Jose
headlines.description: A multiple-vehicle crash early Monday morning killed at least one person and temporarily shut down three northbound lanes on Interstate Highway 280 in San Jose, according to the California Highway Patrol. The crash was first reported at about 5:40 a.m. just north of State Route 87. Around 6:30 a.m., three lanes were closed and traffic was diverted off the freeway. The lanes have since reopened. The CHP did not immediately provide details about the people involved or what caused the crash. Bay City News contributed to this report

headlines.title: Man in Oakland crosswalk killed in suspected hit-and-run collision
headlines.description: Police are investigating an apparent hit-and-run collision that killed a pedestrian in Oakland over the weekend. According to the Oakland Police Department, a man was walking just before 6 a.m. Saturday in a marked crosswalk in the area of 17th Street and Lakeside Drive when a fast-moving vehicle on northbound Lakeside Drive struck him. “When officers arrived, they found an adult male in the intersection on the ground. Officers attempted lifesaving measures, but unfortunately the man died at the scene,” police officials said in a statement. The driver did not stop the vehicle and fled the scene, police said. The suspect has not yet been located, as of 6 a.m. Monday. The victim’s identity was withheld pending next of kin notification. Police also did not immediately confirm if alcohol or drugs were involved in the crash. Anyone with information about the collision is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department Traffic Investigation Unit at 510-777-8570. Any relevant videos or photos can be sent to cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

headlines.title: ‘So scary': Police activity at San Jose theater leaves moviegoers frightened
headlines.description: Moviegoers were left frightened Saturday night after police responded with guns drawn to the AMC Saratoga 14 theater in San Jose. San Jose police said they responded to a report of someone with a gun in theater No. 13. Some moviegoers said the film stopped halfway, the lights went on and police stormed in. “The lights turned on and then the volume lowered,” Lauren, a moviegoer, said. “The police stormed in. There were six cops. One of them was pointing a huge gun at the back of the room and they told the guy in the back right to stand up and put his hands above his head.” Lauren said the theater was nearly full. “We were really scared,” Lauren said. Police said they located a man in the theater matching the description of the man who reportedly had a gun. But he did not have a weapon, and officers did not find a gun. Moviegoer Aditya Gupta said he was stunned when police came in. “The girl who was sitting on my right, she ducked, and I realized after the fact that I should’ve done the same,” he said. “I don’t think it registered to me that there was a real officer with a real assault rifle-looking thing.” He said officers briefly explained to moviegoers why they were there. “One of them was explaining to everybody, ‘Sorry for the disturbance. It’s just that we were told that someone was waving a weapon around,’” Gupta said. Fearing a possible shootout, Gupta said he took off. Lauren said she and her friend left, too. “It was so scary,” Lauren said. “It was scary to see a gun that big right in front of me.” No one was hurt. Lauren said the incident was so frightening that she plans to take a break from going to the movies. NBC Bay Area reached out to AMC for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

headlines.title: What to know about the Kelvin wave raising the sea level along the West Coast
headlines.description: Sea levels along the West Coast will begin to rise by up to a foot this month as a series of pulses of warm water called Kelvin waves hit the shoreline and move north, sparking concerns about beach erosion and flooding in areas already impacted by climate change and El Niño. Kelvin waves are not like tsunamis, and they don’t curl over and crash on the beach. A better image is water sloshing in the bathtub or a swimming pool during an earthquake. In the ocean, they are bulges of water that lift the sea level as they move along the coast. They’re common during El Niño events, but this year’s super El Niño could intensify the impacts, experts say. Over the next week, the 6-inch to foot-tall surge will move north along the California coast at about 6 miles per hour (9.6 kilometers per hour), or 150 miles per day (241 kilometers per day), bringing higher sea levels to Oregon and Washington state. Experts predict the waves will continue to pass through from October until February. “It’s not that this Kelvin wave is going to come and flood anything on its own,” said Michael Jacox, a research oceanographer with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Fisheries’ Ecosystem Science Division. Instead, it raises the baseline. If you start with sea levels that are 6 inches higher than normal, when you have really high tides, big storms or storm surges, the water levels are now 6 inches higher, he said. “The effects can be amplified,” he said. The waves also increase ocean temperatures and push cold, nutrient-rich waters deeper below the surface, which has an impact on marine life. Here’s what to know about Kelvin waves. How does a Kelvin wave form? Kelvin waves are a “fact of life” during an El Niño, a naturally occurring climate pattern involving the warming ocean waters, said Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor in the Department of Marine, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences at North Carolina State University. They form when the trade winds along the equator change direction. Winds blowing east to west along the equator push water in the Pacific Ocean west toward Asia, Jacox said. When those winds weaken or reverse direction, that bulge of water gets pushed back toward the east along the equator until it hits South America. When the surge of water hits the coastline at the equator, it moves north and south along the North and South American coasts. The wave isn’t visible to the naked eye and they won’t cause boats to go up and down, Amaya said. It’s more like a big pancake. It’s wider than it’s deep: The bulge extends 12 to 20 miles (19 to 32 kilometers) off the coast and about 200 meters deep, Amaya said. What are the potential impacts of Kelvin waves? Many coastal communities are already grappling with the impacts of rising sea levels, like the coastal erosion eating away at the beach in San Clemente, California. Waves are also getting bigger, experts say. The higher sea levels could exacerbate those problems. “People are on edge,” Amaya said. “They think about more flooding happening, more beach erosion so when you hear elevated sea states coastal inundation risk, I think that raises a lot of anxiety.” The higher sea level combined with larger than average waves from North Pacific swell, which are expected during the El Niño, plus large spring tides from October to February, can cause exceptional erosion on the West Coast, said Sean Vitousek, a research oceanographer with the U.S. Geological Survey. Generally, the largest El Niño events of 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 caused West Coast beaches to experience their worst erosion on record, Vitousek said. “The loss of protective beaches also increases wave impacts and coastal flooding on property and infrastructure,” he said. Things could intensify over time as more waves arrive over the winter. Typically El Niños are associated with five or six of these waves, Amaya said. During the last major El Niño in 2015-2016 there were five Kelvin waves. One already came through in May or June and there’s evidence of a third Kelvin wave forming, he said. Experts expect it to continue up the coast over the next month or so. How are states responding to concerns about higher sea levels? There’s concern the waves could worsen challenges along the Southern California coast, said Alyssa Napuri, deputy chief of staff for Orange County Supervisor Katrina Foley. Already, waves are approaching a seaside rail line and oceanfront homes were damaged during swells last month tied to Hurricane Marie. Authorities are placing emergency sand on beaches as quickly as possible, Napuri said, adding that forecasts show the Kelvin Wave could send water levels between six to 12 inches higher. “We’re already struggling as it is,” Napuri said. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, proclaimed a state of emergency in late September to prepare the state for what will likely be a historic El Niño season. The proclamation will help the state “move faster to protect communities, stage critical resources, and strengthen readiness before severe weather intensifies,” the governor said in a statement. Experts with the Washington state Department of Natural Resources are ready to respond to any disasters that might come with the Kelvin waves, said spokesperson Courtney James. They regularly coordinate through the state Emergency Management Division but they have not been asked to do any special preparation so far, she said. Actual damages from the Kelvin waves will depend on the storms and tides magnified by El Niño, and if they’re stronger, the damage could be significant, Amaya said. “It’s too too early to be sure whether this particular winter season will be a record breaker in terms of this El Niño, but this El Niño itself is certainly on that trajectory of being one of the largest if not the largest El Niño we’ve ever seen,” he said.

headlines.title: Missing 14-year-old Monterey County teen rescued in Mexico, father arrested
headlines.description: A 14-year-old Monterey County girl who was the subject of an Amber Alert has been rescued in Mexico and her father, who is suspected of sexually abusing her, has been arrested, authorities said. The Monterey County Sheriff’s Office said the teen, whom NBC Bay Area is not naming because she a victim of sexual abuse and a minor, was rescued by Mexican law enforcement. Sheriff Tina Nieto said the teen’s father, 38-year-old Sergio Galvez Perez, was arrested after he was allegedly found in possession of narcotics. Galvez Perez is wanted on several felony charges, including incest, lewd or lascivious acts with a child under 14, unlawful sexual intercourse and child endangerment. Nieto said Mexican authorities are aware of Galvez Perez’s pending charges in Monterey County, and worked with local police and the FBI to rescue the girl. “[She] is safe and is currently in the care of local authorities in Mexico,” Nieto added. The announcement comes almost a month after the California Highway Patrol issued an Amber Alert for the teen and her father. The alert was issued amid an investigation into the remains of an infant found on Aug. 1 on the side of a road in Monterey County. It’s not clear how the infant died, but investigators said infant’s body showed signs of traumatic injury. Investigators eventually identified Galvaz Perez and the teen as being connected to the newborn, which authorities have named “Baby Angelita.” The sheriff’s office said they believe the 14-year-old conceived the child as a result of her father’s sexual abuse, gave birth on the side of a road and left the baby. While the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office had initially said the teen girl was wanted on suspicion of murder, the District Attorney’s Office said no charging decision had been made. “We recognize that the 14-year-old is a victim of her father’s abuse. No child should ever have to endure such horrific circumstances,” the DA’s office said in part in a statement on Sept. 2. “Our office works with victims of abuse every day and understands that children who have experienced abuse can face extraordinary barriers to safety and may be unable to seek help on their own, particularly when they are under the control or influence of an abuser. The responsibility for getting a child to safety does not rest on the child. Our priority is to ensure that this young girl is safe and has access to the support and services she needs.” The teen’s mother, Ofelia Garcia Ortega, was arrested in August for alleged child endangerment and later released on bail. Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore.
